title: Will the U.S.-DRC Strategic Partnership Agreement Endanger U.S. Interests in the DRC?
gist: Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi is citing Article XII of the December 2025 U.S.-DRC Strategic Partnership Agreement as the justification for a constitutional amendment granting him a third term ahead of the December 2028 election — a claim the text of the agreement does not support and that Washington has not rebutted. Neema argues that U.S. silence, driven by its appetite for critical minerals and its contest with China, is converting a commercial deal into cover for a regime-preservation scheme that would layer a Kinshasa-centered political crisis onto the eastern war, raise DRC country risk, and ultimately price American companies out of the very minerals Washington is chasing.

themes.theme: SPA Article XII as political pretext

insights.claim: Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi is invoking the U.S.-DRC Strategic Partnership Agreement signed in December 2025 as a required justification for amending the constitution to grant himself a third term ahead of the December 2028 general election.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: The single biggest political-risk catalyst in DRC through 2028 is now formally tethered to a U.S. commercial agreement; anyone underwriting Congolese mining exposure is implicitly underwriting a constitutional crisis.
insights.locator: The Democratic Republic of the Congo’s (DRC) next general election

insights.claim: Article XII of the U.S.-DRC Strategic Partnership Agreement commits Kinshasa to take all necessary measures — including constitutional amendments — within twelve months of signing, but never specifies the nature or purpose of any constitutional change, creating deliberate interpretive room.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: Vague legal drafting in resource-for-partnership deals is itself a risk factor: it hands host-country incumbents a foreign-policy alibi for domestic power grabs.
insights.locator: In invoking the U.S.-DRC SPA, the Congolese president

insights.claim: The obligations actually named in Paragraph 2(a) of Article XII — amending Law No. 13/005 of 11 February 2014 on the fiscal, customs, parafiscal, non-tax revenue and exchange regime — require only changes to the DRC's fiscal law and mining code, not to its constitution.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: The legal case for a third term collapses on inspection — meaning the constitutional push is discretionary politics, not treaty compliance, and can still be reversed by explicit U.S. pushback.
insights.quote: To align with the SPA, the DRC would have to refine its fiscal law and its mining code, but not its constitution.
insights.locator: The ambiguity created by the DRC’s vague commitment

insights.claim: Tshisekedi presented the constitutional amendment as a Washington-imposed condition at a Kinshasa press conference on May 6, 2026 without offering any evidence, and the United States has never substantiated or responded to the claim.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: A cost-free U.S. denial has gone unissued for nearly three months — the clearest tell that Washington is trading acquiescence for mineral access.
insights.quote: The United States has not substantiated or responded to Tshisekedi’s claims.
insights.locator: During a press conference held in Kinshasa on May 6, 2026

insights.claim: By letting a commercial agreement be cited as the reason for a constitutional rewrite, Washington is made a de facto accomplice to a foreign leader's bid to stay in power, without ever having agreed to that role.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: Transactional bilateral deals carry an unpriced reputational liability: the counterparty can unilaterally assign you political ownership of its domestic agenda.
insights.quote: By instrumentalizing the SPA, Tshisekedi is drawing Washington into the country’s domestic political debate and making it a de facto accomplice to his political ambitions
insights.locator: It therefore appears that the Congolese government

insights.claim: Kinshasa reads U.S. demand for critical minerals as the currency that buys the Trump administration's protection against the DRC's enemies, turning mineral access into an explicit political bargaining chip.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: Supply agreements struck on this logic are only as durable as the incumbent regime — a leadership change can void the whole mineral thesis overnight.
insights.locator: Meeting Washington’s expectations—access to critical minerals

insights.claim: The unaddressed quid pro quo sustaining the U.S.-DRC agreement — critical minerals in exchange for political support — will itself trigger a political crisis in the DRC that compounds the existing war in the east.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: The deal is self-undermining: the arrangement meant to secure supply is the mechanism that destabilizes it.
insights.locator: If left unaddressed, the apparent quid pro quo

insights.claim: Even silent U.S. support for a regime that prioritizes American companies over Chinese competitors is geopolitically appealing in the short run but carries far greater risk to long-term U.S. interests in the DRC.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: The short-horizon trade (secure offtake now) and the long-horizon trade (stable producing state) are in direct conflict — position sizing should reflect which horizon the policy is actually serving.
insights.quote: Washington’s silence regarding Tshisekedi’s ambitions could easily be interpreted as tacit support for the regime.
insights.locator: From a geopolitical standpoint, even silently supporting a regime

insights.claim: By allowing the Strategic Partnership Agreement to be manipulated in a way that deepens Congolese political crisis, the Trump administration is working against the agreement's own stated objectives.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: Watch for policy incoherence as a leading indicator that a flagship bilateral deal will underdeliver on volumes.
insights.locator: When the Trump administration allows the SPA to be manipulated

themes.theme: Country risk and the crowding-out of U.S. capital

insights.claim: A Congolese political crisis would elevate the country's risk profile enough to deter U.S. companies from investing, because American corporates historically require lower risk than the DRC's instability permits.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: Rising DRC political risk mechanically shifts marginal mining capex away from U.S.-listed operators and toward higher-risk-tolerance foreign bidders.
insights.locator: Such a crisis would elevate the country’s risk profile

insights.claim: A 1982 U.S. Congressional Budget Office report on cobalt policy already documented that political instability in Zaire threatened the U.S. cobalt supply chain and hindered investment — the same dynamic now recurring four decades later.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: The cobalt-supply-vs-Congolese-instability linkage is a 40-year recurring pattern, not a novel risk — history argues against assuming this cycle resolves differently.
insights.locator: A 1982 report on cobalt policy

insights.claim: For companies from third countries with a much higher risk appetite than American firms, a high-risk DRC environment is an opportunity because it eliminates U.S. corporate competition for assets.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: Instability in the DRC is not symmetrically bad — it is a relative-value transfer to Chinese and other risk-tolerant miners, which is precisely the outcome U.S. policy claims to be preventing.
insights.quote: for companies from some third countries with a much higher risk appetite than American companies, a high-risk environment will present an opportunity by eliminating potential U.S. corporate competition
insights.locator: Meanwhile, for companies from some third countries

insights.claim: Long-term political stability in the DRC would lower the country's risk profile and give U.S. investors the incentive to commit over longer time horizons, making democracy promotion an economic instrument rather than a values exercise.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: Reframes governance conditionality as a discount-rate argument: cost of capital, not idealism, is the case for opposing the amendment.
insights.locator: Long-term political stability will lower the country’s risk profile

themes.theme: Mispriced risk: Kinshasa, not the east

insights.claim: The DRC risk that investors, insurers, and Washington have already priced is the eastern war; the genuinely unpriced risk is broader political instability centered on Kinshasa, where decisions are actually made.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: The headline conflict is in the price; the capital-city political risk is not — that asymmetry is where the surprise, and the repricing, will come from.
insights.quote: The instability in the DRC that should concern Washington is not the war in the east.
insights.locator: Identifying the Risks

insights.claim: Neither the U.S. administration nor the companies betting on the Strategic Partnership Agreement have factored in the combination of a contested third term layered onto the eastern war and multiple other rebel movements and armed groups radiating outward from the capital.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: Explicit claim of a market/policy blind spot — the trade is being short the assumption that DRC risk stays compartmentalized in the east.

insights.claim: In copper- and cobalt-rich Katanga, long-brewing and recently intensifying ethnic tensions between autochthones aligned with Moïse Katumbi and Joseph Kabila and migrating populations from Tshisekedi's home region of Kasai could ignite unprecedented violence if he tries to cling to power.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: The specific flashpoint sits directly on top of global copper and cobalt production — the transmission channel from Congolese politics to battery-metal supply is geographic and immediate.
insights.quote: Tshisekedi’s attempt to cling to power could ignite unprecedented violence.
insights.locator: In regions like copper- and cobalt-rich Katanga

insights.claim: The Congolese opposition's June 3, 2026 'ville morte,' which partially shut down Kinshasa and other cities, was an early demonstration of mobilization capacity against a third term.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated escalation marker — frequency and reach of ville morte actions is the cheapest real-time gauge of crisis trajectory.

insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: The regime's repressive capacity is thinner than in the last cycle, raising the odds that a crisis escalates beyond containment rather than being suppressed.

insights.claim: Against the uncertainties of an amendment and extended Tshisekedi rule stands the quasi-certainty of a predictable, peaceful transition carried out on constitutional deadlines — the first-ever DRC succession between two ballot-elected presidents.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: Frames the choice as trading a knowable, dateable base case for an unbounded tail — the classic setup for mispriced political risk.

themes.theme: Silence as engagement in U.S.-China mineral competition

insights.claim: A U.S. policy of not commenting on foreign elections cannot survive contact with great-power mineral competition, because Washington would not stay indifferent if Congolese political change produced an openly pro-China, anti-U.S. leader.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: Declared non-interference is not a constraint you can trade on — expect discretionary U.S. intervention the moment the leadership outcome turns unfavorable.
insights.quote: the realpolitik is that Washington has a stake in who leads the DRC.
insights.locator: Is the U.S. Silence Principled or Just Opportunistic?

insights.claim: U.S. silence in the DRC is not neutrality but a form of engagement rooted in a geopolitical calculation about who holds power — one Washington is unlikely ever to acknowledge.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: Read official silence on Congolese constitutional questions as an active policy signal, not an absence of one.
insights.quote: So, silence itself becomes a form of engagement in the DRC’s politics that the United States is unlikely to acknowledge.
insights.locator: Even if the Trump administration’s silence on this matter

themes.theme: Precedent, sanctions, and the coherence trap

insights.claim: From 2014 to 2018, across the Obama administration and Trump's first term, senior U.S. officials including Secretary of State John Kerry and Great Lakes envoys Russ Feingold and Tom Perriello repeatedly and on a bipartisan basis pressed Kabila not to seek a third term.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: Establishes that opposing DRC term extension was long-standing bipartisan practice, making current silence a discrete break rather than continuity.
insights.locator: From 2014 to 2018—a very different era

insights.claim: During a 2017 Kinshasa visit, then-UN Ambassador Nikki Haley delivered the first Trump administration's explicit opposition to constitutional revision and election delays, as confirmed in November 2017 House testimony by acting assistant secretary Donald Yamamoto.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: The same administration brand has an on-record position against exactly what it is now tolerating — a documented inconsistency that advocacy and Congress can weaponize.
insights.quote: a clear message to President Kabila and his government that further delays and an unrealistic electoral calendar would be unacceptable
insights.locator: Subsequently, during a 2017 visit to Kinshasa

insights.claim: When the U.S. sanctioned Joseph Kabila on April 30, 2026, it chose to cite his decade-old election delays even though his alleged M23 ties alone would have justified the designation — voluntarily making electoral manipulation part of its own DRC standard.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: Washington created its own precedent trap in 2026; the sanctions rationale is the lever for forcing a public U.S. position on Tshisekedi's amendment.
insights.locator: This U.S. administration, of its own accord

insights.claim: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's stated standard for the Kabila sanction — that those who continue to sow instability will be held accountable — logically applies to a contested constitutional amendment opposed by the opposition and civil society amid an active eastern rebellion.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: Sanctions language sets a testable benchmark — failure to apply it to Tshisekedi is the marker that mineral access has overridden stated policy.
insights.quote: President Trump is paving the way for peace in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and he has been clear that those who continue to sow instability will be held accountable.
insights.locator: In the press release announcing the U.S. sanction on Kabila

insights.claim: Unlike Kabila's regime, which Washington merely suspected of seeking a term extension, Tshisekedi's has openly declared its intention to amend the constitution and remain in power — making the case against it easier, not harder.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: Removes the ambiguity defense: U.S. inaction cannot be attributed to uncertainty about intent.

insights.claim: A layered political crisis on top of the security crisis would defeat the diplomatic architecture the U.S. has built in the DRC — the December 2025 Washington Accords for Peace and Prosperity, African Union initiatives, and the Doha process — and undercut Trump's peacemaker narrative in Africa.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
entities: Washington Accords for Peace and Prosperity
insights.so_what: The peace framework underpinning any DRC investment case is contingent on the constitutional question being resolved cleanly.
insights.locator: Peacemaker Turned Crisis-Enabler

insights.claim: Backing a compliant Congolese strongman is neither stable nor defensible, as the manner of Mobutu Sese Seko's fall and the chaos that followed demonstrate, even though a covertly U.S.-backed Tshisekedi looks good for Washington in the near term.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: The Mobutu precedent is the base rate for how patron-client mineral arrangements in the DRC end — abruptly, and with assets stranded.
insights.locator: Some may argue that all these concerns are just possibilities

insights.claim: The strategic objectives of securing critical-minerals access and competing with China take multiple decades to achieve, while the consequences of Congolese political instability outlast U.S. electoral cycles — so framing the stakes within one administration's time horizon is a category error.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: Mineral-security strategies priced on four-year political cycles will systematically underinvest in the stability that determines whether supply actually arrives.
insights.quote: the stability of producing states like the DRC must be understood as a long-term interest, not a line item to be traded away for short-term access.
insights.locator: Finally, it is important to resist the temptation

insights.claim: Publicly opposing any constitutional amendment granting Tshisekedi a third term would depersonalize the Strategic Partnership Agreement, positioning the U.S. as a partner of the Congolese state rather than of a particular regime and de-incentivizing actors who threaten stability.
insights.speaker: Christian-Géraud Neema
insights.so_what: The prescribed fix is cheap and verifiable — a public U.S. statement — so its absence should be treated as informative about actual U.S. priorities.
insights.locator: The United States could contribute to peace and stability
